en: The Sūtra on the Samādhi of the Array of Powers, Volume One.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Narendrayaśas of India during the Sui Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Bhagavān was dwelling in the city of Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove.
At the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park, he was together with a community of five hundred bhikṣus;
all were great arhats whose outflows were exhausted, who were free from further afflictions,
whose minds were well-liberated and whose wisdom was well-liberated, whose hearts were as gentle as tamed elephants, and who were pure both internally and externally.
Having ultimately cast off the heavy burden of the five aggregates, they have accomplished what was to be done and will not undergo further existence;
like the unconditioned liberation of the Buddhas, they are no longer subject to the conditioned flux of birth and death—
with the sole exception of one person remaining on the stage of training, namely the Elder Bhikṣu Ānanda— all [others] were thus.
All have attained the dharma of quiescence; all have attained the dharma of subduing; all are fully endowed with the most supreme dharma;
none abide within the realm of consciousness; all have attained various forms of liberation;
and all have attained sovereign supernormal powers.
Furthermore, there were eighty hundred thousand bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who served as leaders, namely:
the youth Mañjuśrī; the youth Jñānacakra-sāgara-pratibhāna; the youth Padmagarbha-raśmi-sarvasattvacakṣus;
the youth Anantacitta-vipula-artha-jñāna; and the youth Deva-ratnārcis.
The youth Banner of Radiant Good Illumination; the youth Delightful Vision of Incomparable Color;
the youth Gazing at All Sentient Beings with Unblinking Eyes; the youth Vision of Great Vows Never Failing;
the youth Resounding Drum-Sound of Deep and Distant Thunder; and the youth Eye of All Sentient Beings Free from Obstruction.
The youth Ratnagarbhajvālācakravipulaguṇa, the youth Bahupuṇyasattvadṛṣṭavijayadhvaja,
the youth Vijayānantagandhaprabha, the youth Anantabalavīryasuvikrānta,
the youth Dṛḍhavīryānantajñānārcidhvaja, and the youth Sarvaviśeṣaguṇavijñāna.
O Youth, you who are indestructible and eternally supreme; O Youth, accomplished master of all sovereign powers;
O Youth, adorned with the marks and signs of excellence, pure in meritorious conduct, and of excellent renown;
O Youth, most beloved by all sentient beings.

Together with this assembly of youths, they all attained the path of non-retrogression. Adorned by the great vows of the adamantine armor, their minds were ever tranquil; they reached the end of all existence and attained great purity, supreme purity, ultimate purity, and the purity of all pure practices within the indestructible Dharma.
At that time, during the first watch of the latter part of the night, the World-Honored One entered a samādhi called "Array of Power.
Having entered this samādhi, he fully knew the karmic actions and the cycles of birth and death of all sentient beings throughout the past, present, and future.

By the spiritual power of the Buddha, at that moment, this site of the Jeta Grove and the entire expanse of space were completely filled with celestial robes and jeweled canopies, interlaced with nets and lattices;
celestial parasols, banners, and streamers crowded together everywhere;
furthermore, various kinds of exquisite tassels and fine filaments hung down, while celestial flowers fell in profusion and in disarray.
The forest trees were interspersed and set with the seven treasures, and various ornaments were strewn upon the ground;

celestial fragrant leaves, celestial *mīnāra*, celestial *candana*, *kunkuma*, and incense smoke formed dense, subtle clouds that hung low and swirled in profusion, sometimes curling and sometimes unfolding—lovely and delightful to behold.

At that time, the Jeta Grove was thus adorned with various kinds of celestial jewels; because it was so vast and pure, it possessed great majesty and virtue, endowed with manifold radiance that illuminated the void throughout the ten directions.
Having manifested these immeasurable adornments, a lion throne spontaneously appeared, extraordinary, exquisite, and perfected by superior celestial retribution.

By reason of the light from the adornments of this throne, this entire trichiliocosm was made brilliantly radiant and illuminated; it was as if a great torch were lit in the night, such that all darkness was extinguished without remainder.

At that time, all the impurities of this Sahā world-system of three thousand great thousand worlds—including hills, mounds, cliffs, riverbanks, plains, gravel, sand, high and low pits and hollows, ponds, ditches, ravines, springs, wells, rivers, lakes, small streams, great rivers, small seas, and great oceans; as well as Mount Sumeru, the islands of the sea, the ten-jeweled mountains where the sages and seers dwell such as Nimindhara, Mount Cakravāḍa, and Mahācakravāḍa—all became level and even. Devoid of thorns and other thickets, they were pure and flat like the palm of a lapis lazuli hand.

Furthermore, there were various adornments of the seven treasures, and celestial *mandārava* flowers covered the ground everywhere. Celestial lotus leaves and roots, celestial *tamāla*, and celestial cinnamon and saffron incense formed fragrant clouds that pervaded and circled the entire expanse of space.

Moreover, immeasurable music from the various devas—consisting of hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of *nayutas* of kinds—spontaneously produced sounds that all proclaimed the sublime Dharma.

At that time, this trichiliocosm was filled with various lotus flowers made of the seven precious gems, adorning the entirety of space. Their most excellent fragrant light was all golden in color; they had stems of pure blue lapis lazuli, with calyxes seven cubits wide and seven fathoms high. The lotuses were in full bloom, exceedingly delightful;

there were celestial sandalwood trees, *mandārava* flower trees, and celestial *nāga-puṣpa* trees, each tree seven *tāla* trees high, with spreading branches and leaves, perfect in color and fragrance, in blue, yellow, red, and white, all like the lotus flowers.

In this way, he adorned the three-thousandfold great thousandfold world-system—from the entire realm of earth up to the Peak of Existence—so that it was entirely like a celestial palace, a pure and wondrous land.

Having manifested this transformation, at that time all immeasurable sentient beings, through the empowerment of the Buddha’s power, were without obstruction; they could see each other clearly as if through pure lapis lazuli, for the realm of the Buddha is difficult to conceive.

At that time, the gods dwelling on the earth of this trichiliocosm, up to all the gods of the Akaniṣṭha heaven, as well as the assembly of five hundred arhat bhikṣus and eight million bodhisattvas, had this thought:

“This is the power of the Tathāgata’s adornment; this is the Tathāgata, the lion among men; this is the Tathāgata’s greatest prowess; this is the Tathāgata’s lion-like prowess; this is the Tathāgata’s great, great lion-like prowess and leaping exultation; this is the Tathāgata’s great, great adornment of supernormal powers—an inconceivable and ineffable matter.”

Having seen this, the entire great assembly—the devas, śrāvakas, bodhisattvas, and others—conceived great faith toward the Buddha; they knelt with their right knees on the ground, joined their palms, and remained there with single-minded devotion, bowing their heads in worship.

At that time, to the east, beyond worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River, there was a buddha-field named Sarvālokā. In it dwelt a Buddha named Anantaprabha, a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, together with a great assembly of eight million bhikṣus, thirty million bhikṣuṇīs, eighty hundred ten-million bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, eight hundred and eighty thousand upāsakas, and seven hundred ten-million upāsikās. There were also gods and humans of supreme majesty and virtue, all surrounding the Buddha’s seat within that assembly to listen to his exposition of the essential Dharma.

At that time, to the south, beyond worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River, there was a buddha-field named Great Radiance (*Mahāprabha*). Therein dwelt a Buddha named Boundless Diligence (*Anantavīrya*), a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, together with a great assembly of ten billion bhikṣus, forty million bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, and sixty million upāsakas. There were also gods and humans of supreme majesty and virtue, all surrounding the Buddha’s seat within that assembly, listening to him expound the essential points of the Dharma.

At that time, to the west, beyond worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, there was a buddha-field named Samantaprabhā. In it dwelt a Buddha named Samantadarśin, a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, together with a great assembly of twenty million bhikṣus, thirty million bhikṣuṇīs, nine hundred and sixty million bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, eighty million upāsakas, and sixty million upāsikās. There were also gods and humans of supreme majesty and virtue who all surrounded the Buddha’s seat within that assembly, listening to him preach the essentials of the Dharma.

At that time, to the north, beyond worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, there was a buddha-field named Great Lamp. In it dwelt a Buddha named Kārakaprabhā, a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, together with a great assembly of six hundred million bhikṣus, forty thousand bhikṣuṇīs, eight hundred million bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, nine hundred million upāsakas, and eight hundred million upāsikās. There were also gods and humans of supreme majesty and virtue, all surrounding the Buddha’s seat within that assembly, listening to him preach the essentials of the Dharma.

At that time, to the northeast, beyond worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River, there was a buddha-field named Golden Light Radiance. Therein dwelt a Buddha named Golden Light Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, together with a great assembly of seven hundred million bhikṣus, three hundred million bhikṣuṇīs, eight hundred million bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, nine hundred million upāsakas, and eight hundred million upāsikās. There were also gods and humans of supreme majesty and virtue; all surrounded the Buddha’s seat within that assembly, listening to him preach the essential points of the Dharma.

At that time, to the southeast, beyond worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River, there was a buddha-field named Great Torch Light (*Mahārcis*). In it dwelt a Buddha named Inconceivable Sunlight (*Acintyasuryaprabha*)—a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha—who was surrounded by a great assembly of eight hundred and forty million bhikṣus, one hundred and eighty million bhikṣuṇīs, nine hundred and sixty million bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, eight hundred and eighty million upāsakas, and eight hundred million upāsikās. There were also gods and humans of supreme majesty and virtue, all gathered around the Buddha’s seat to listen to his exposition of the essential Dharma.

At that time, to the southwest, past worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River, there was a buddha-field named Supravara-prabha. In it dwelt a Buddha named Mahāprabha, a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, together with a great assembly of ninety-six million bhikṣus, eighty million bhikṣuṇīs, ninety-two million bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, ninety million upāsakas, and ninety-six million upāsikās. There were also gods and humans of supreme majesty and virtue, all surrounding the Buddha’s seat within that assembly, listening to him preach the essentials of the Dharma.

At that time, to the northwest, beyond worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, there was a buddha-field named Ratnajñānamati. In it dwelt a Buddha named Ratnagarbhaprabhāsa, a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, together with a great assembly of eight hundred million bhikṣus, two hundred million bhikṣuṇīs, eight hundred million bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, eighty-eight million upāsakas, and seven hundred million upāsikās. There were also gods and humans of supreme majesty and virtue, all surrounding the Buddha’s seat within that assembly, listening to him expound the essential points of the Dharma.

At that time, above, beyond worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, there was a buddha-field named Sun-Moon Radiance. In it dwelt a Buddha named Moon-Standard Radiance (*Candradhvaja-prabha*), a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, together with a great assembly of one billion bhikṣus, three hundred million bhikṣuṇīs, eight hundred million bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, nine hundred and twenty million upāsakas, and nine hundred million upāsikās. There were also gods and humans of supreme majesty and virtue, all surrounding the Buddha’s seat within that assembly, listening to him preach the essentials of the Dharma.

At that time, below this world, past as many worlds as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, there was a buddha-field named Vimalaprabhā. In it dwelt a Buddha named Samantacakṣudarśana, a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, together with a great assembly of ninety-six million bhikṣus, forty million bhikṣuṇīs, ninety-four million bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, eighty million upāsakas, and seventy million upāsikās. There were also gods and humans of supreme majesty and virtue, all surrounding the Buddha’s seat within that assembly, listening to him preach the essential Dharma.
At that time, the youth Mañjuśrī and the youth Sarvasattvapriyadarśana—these twenty youths together—simultaneously rose and went to where the Buddha was.
Having arrived at the Buddha’s abode, Śākyamuni Buddha was in samādhi, adorned with the hundred blessings, serene and unmoving. At that time, the youths each remained silent;

they bared their right shoulders, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and circumambulated the Tathāgata three times to the right. Then, in the time it takes a strong man to bend and extend his arm, they each departed for the ten directions.

At that time, the youth Mañjuśrī and the youth Jñānacakra-sāgara-pratibhāna traveled toward the eastern direction, passing through as many lands as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River. There they found a world named Sarvālokā, wherein dwelt a Buddha named Anantaprabha Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha—fully endowed with the ten titles—who was preaching the subtle and wondrous Dharma for the great assembly.
When the two youths had arrived at that land, they paid homage to the Buddha and sat among the assembly.

At that time, the youth Lotus-Treasury-Light-All-Sentient-Beings-Eye and the youth Boundless-Mind-Vast-Meaning-Wisdom, and others, traveled toward the southern direction, passing through lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River. There was a world there named Great Light, wherein dwelt a Buddha named Boundless Diligence Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha—fully endowed with the ten titles—who was preaching the subtle and wondrous Dharma for the great assembly.
When the two youths had arrived at that land, they paid homage to the Buddha and sat among the assembly.

At that time, the youth Celestial Jewel Radiant Light Well-illuminating Banner and the youth Incomparable Color Lovely to Behold, together with others, traveled toward the western direction across as many lands as there are sands in the Ganges River. There was a world there named Universal Light, wherein dwelt a Buddha named Universal Vision, a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha—fully endowed with the ten titles—who was preaching the subtle and wondrous Dharma for the great assembly.
When the two youths had arrived at that land, they paid homage to the Buddha and sat among the assembly.

At that time, the youth named Observing All Sentient Beings with Unblinking Eyes and the youth named Great Vow Not Seen in Vain and others traveled toward the north, passing through as many lands as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River. There was a world there called Great Lamp, wherein dwelt a Buddha named Light-Maker Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha—complete with the ten titles—who was preaching the subtle and wondrous Dharma for the great assembly.
When the two youths had reached that land, they paid homage to the Buddha and sat among the assembly.

At that time, the youth Deep-Resounding Drum-Sound Like Thunder and the youth Freeing All Sentient Beings from Obstructions in Their Eyes, and others like them, traveled toward the northeast across as many lands as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River. There was a world there named Golden Radiance, wherein dwelt a Buddha named Golden Light Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha—fully endowed with the ten titles—who was preaching the subtle and wondrous Dharma for the great assembly.
When the two youths had arrived at that land, they paid homage to the Buddha and sat among the assembly.

At that time, the youth Ratnagarbhajvālācakravideha, the youth Bahubalavantasattvadṛṣṭivaijayanta, and the others traveled toward the southeast, passing through lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. There was a world there called Mahājvālāloka, where dwelt a Buddha named Acintyādityaprabhā Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha—fully endowed with the ten titles—who was preaching the subtle and wondrous Dharma for the great assembly.
When the two youths had arrived at that land, they paid homage to the Buddha and sat among the assembly.

At that time, the youth Boundless Fragrant Light of Supreme Wonder and the youth Great Exertion of Boundless Power and Vigor, and others, traveled toward the southwest, passing through as many lands as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River. There was a world there named Good Victorious Light, wherein dwelt a Buddha named Great Light Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha—fully endowed with the ten titles—who was preaching the subtle and wondrous Dharma for the great assembly.
When the two youths had arrived at that land, they paid homage to the Buddha and sat among the assembly.

At that time, the youth Firm Vigor Boundless Wisdom Light Banner and the youth Supreme Wisdom of All Distinct Virtues, together with their retinues, traveled toward the northwest, passing through as many lands as there are sands in the Ganges River. There was a world there named Jewel Mind Wisdom, where a Buddha named Jewel Treasury Light Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha—endowed with the ten titles—was preaching the subtle and wondrous Dharma for a great multitude.
When the two youths had arrived at that land, they paid homage to the Buddha and sat among the assembly.

At that time, the youth Indestructible Ever-Supreme and the youth Master Accomplished in All Sovereignities, and others like them, traveled upward through lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. There was a world there named Moonlight and Sunlight, where a Buddha named Ratnaketu-prabha Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha—fully endowed with the ten titles—was preaching the subtle and wondrous Dharma for the great assembly.
When the two youths had arrived at that land, they paid homage to the Buddha and sat among the assembly.

At that time, the youth Adorned with the Marks and Signs of Pure Meritorious Conduct and Good Renown, the youth Most Beloved by All Sentient Beings, and the others, proceeded toward the direction below, passing through as many lands as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River. Therein was a world named Vimalaprabhā (Stainless Light), where dwelt a Buddha named Samantacakṣudarśana Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha—fully endowed with the ten titles—who was preaching the subtle and wondrous Dharma for the great assembly.
When the two youths had arrived at that land, they paid homage to the Buddha and sat among the assembly.

At that time, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Anantaprabha, knowing the thoughts of the great multitude, intentionally addressed the youth Mañjuśrī and the youth Prajñācakrasāgarapratibhāna, saying:
"From where have you two Great Beings come?"
Then the two youths replied to that Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

To the west of this land, passing through worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River, there is a realm named Sahā. Its Buddha is named Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha; he has entered into samādhi by means of great adornments. We have come here after having paid our respects, prostrating ourselves, and circumambulating him three times at the presence of that Buddha, the World-Honored One.”

At that time, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Anantavīrya, knowing [the thoughts] of the great assembly, intentionally asked the youth Padmagarbhaprabhasarvasattvacakṣus and the youth Anantacittavipulārthamati:
"From where have you two Great Beings come?"
Then the two youths replied to that Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

To the north of this land, passing through worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River, there is a realm named Sahā. Its Buddha is named Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha; he has entered into a samādhi of great adornment. We have come from the presence of that Buddha, the World-Honored One, having paid him respectful homage by bowing our heads and circumambulating him three times.”

At that time, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Sarvadarśin, knowing [the thoughts] of the great assembly, intentionally asked the youth Divyaratnaprabhāsasudarśanadhvaja and the youth Durupamavarṇapriyadarśana and the others:
"From where have you two Great Beings come?"
Then the two youths replied to that Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!

To the east of this land, passing through worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River, there is a realm named Sahā. Its Buddha is named Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha. He has entered into samādhi with great adornments; we have come from the presence of that Buddha, the World-Honored One, having paid him respectful homage by bowing our heads and circumambulating him three times."

At that time, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Great Lamp, knowing full well, intentionally questioned the two youths—Sarvasattvapriyadarśana (Beholding All Beings with Unblinking Eyes) and Mahāpraṇidhānāvañcanadarśana (Beholding the Non-falsity of Great Vows)—and the rest of the great assembly, saying:
"From where have you two Great Beings come?"
Then the two youths replied to that Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

To the south of this land, passing through worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River, there is a realm named Sahā, where the Buddha is called Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha. He has entered into samādhi by means of great adornments; we have come from the presence of that Buddha, the World-Honored One, having paid our respects with prostrations and circumambulated him three times.”

At that time, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Golden Radiance addressed the two great beings, the youth Deep-Resounding Drum-Sound Like Thunder and the youth Unobstructed Eye of All Sentient Beings, knowing full well yet asking them:
"From where have you two great beings come?"
Then the two youths replied to that Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

To the southwest of this land, passing through worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River, there is a realm named Sahā. There dwells a Buddha titled Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, who has entered into samādhi by means of great adornments. We have come here from the presence of that Buddha, the World-Honored One, after having respectfully prostrated and circumambulated him three times.”

At that time, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Sunlight of Inconceivable Radiance, knowing full well, intentionally asked the youth Jewel-Treasury Flame-Wheel Vast Virtue and the youth Supreme Banner Seen by Beings of Great Merit and others, saying:
"From where have you two great beings come?"
Then the two youths replied to that Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

To the northwest of this land, passing through worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River, there is a realm named Sahā. Its Buddha is named Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha; he has entered into samādhi by means of great adornments. We have come from the presence of that Buddha, the World-Honored One, having paid him respectful homage, prostrated ourselves, and circumambulated him three times.”

At that time, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Suprabha, knowing [the answer] yet intentionally questioning the youth Anantagandhaprabhaśrī and the youth Anantabalavīryasuvikrama, and the rest of the great assembly, said:
"From where have you two Great Beings come?"
Then the two youths replied to that Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!

To the northeast of this world-system, passing through worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River, there is a land named Sahā. There, the Buddha is named Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha; he has entered into samādhi by means of great adornments. We have come from the presence of that Buddha, the World-Honored One, having paid him respectful homage, prostrated ourselves, and circumambulated him three times."

At that time, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Ratnagarbhaprabhāsa, knowing full well, intentionally asked the youths Dṛḍhavīryānantajñānārci-ketu and Sarvaviśeṣaguṇajyeṣṭhajñāna and the rest of the great assembly:
"From where have you two Great Beings come?"
Then the two youths replied to that Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

To the southeast of this land, passing through worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River, there is a realm named Sahā. There dwells a Buddha titled Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, who has entered into samādhi by means of great adornments. We have come from the presence of that Buddha, the World-Honored One, having paid him respectful homage, prostrated ourselves, and circumambulated him three times.”

At that time, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Ratnaketuprabhāsa, knowing full well, intentionally asked the two youths—the indestructible and eternally supreme youth Anābhedyapratihārya and the youth Sarvavaśitāsamudgataguru—their words being:
"From where have you two great beings come?"
Then the two youths replied to that Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

Below this world-system, past as many worlds as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, there is a land named Sahā. Its Buddha is named Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha; he has entered into samādhi through great adornments. We have come here after having respectfully prostrated to and circumambulated that Buddha, the World-Honored One, three times.”

At that time, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Universal Eye, knowing full well, intentionally addressed the youth Well-Adorned with Pure Meritorious Deeds and Good Renown, the youth Most Beloved by All Sentient Beings, and the rest of the great assembly, saying:
"From where have you two Great Beings come?"
Then the two youths replied to that Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!

Above this realm, past worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, there is a land named Sahā, where the Buddha is named Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha. He has entered into samādhi through great adornments; we have come here after having respectfully prostrated before that Buddha, the World-Honored One, and circumambulated him three times."

At that time, throughout the worlds of the ten directions, upon hearing the names of these ten titles of Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, all the Buddha-fields in those ten directions shook greatly—shaking, shaking everywhere, shaking equally everywhere; trembling, trembling everywhere, trembling equally everywhere; surging, surging everywhere, surging equally everywhere. Having shaken in this way, the attendants of the Buddhas in those ten directions each joined their palms and addressed their respective Buddhas, saying:
“World-Honored One!...”
"For what cause and condition does this trichiliocosm shake so violently?
At that time, the Buddhas of the ten directions all addressed their respective attendants, saying:
"Virtuous sons!..."

To the west of this land, passing through worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River, there is a realm named Sahā. There, the Buddha is known as Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha; he is currently present, having entered the Samādhi of the Array of Power, seated amidst the fourfold assembly, desiring to expound the profound and equal Dharma.
"Because of this matter, the earth throughout this trichiliocosm shakes and trembles.
In this manner, the shaking of all lands down to the lower directions was likewise.
At that time, the Buddhas of the ten directions again addressed the great assembly of bhikṣus and others, saying:
"You should know this:
it is difficult for a Buddha to appear in the world; to encounter one after he has appeared is even more difficult than that."
Among such hardships, this [task] is a hundred million times more difficult than that of Śākyamuni Tathāgata.

Why is this? Because by the power of the vows and causal conditions from his past lives, that Buddha, the World-Honored One, was born into a defiled land of the five turbidities; such a thing is most difficult.
"O Bhikṣus! Furthermore, that Tathāgata’s name is not uttered in vain.

If all sentient beings within the Buddha-fields of the lands of the ten directions hear of this Śākyamuni Tathāgata’s courageous diligence, his difficult ascetic practices, and the various merits and complete names of the great vows he made in past lives and the difficult deeds performed during his bodhisattva conduct, they shall all attain them."

Having heard this, incalculable and immeasurable sentient beings within all the Buddha-fields of the ten directions all received the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; how much more so those others who attained the fruits of *srotāpanna*, *sakṛdāgāmin*, *anāgāmin*, and *arhat*?

"Therefore, monks, when this great renown of the Tathāgata Śākyamuni is proclaimed, all the Buddhas within all the three-thousandfold world-systems, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges throughout the ten directions, each praise the immeasurable merits of the Tathāgata Śākyamuni—the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha—in this very manner.

That sound is heard again beyond other worlds in the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; in yet more Buddha-fields, equal in number to those same sands of the Ganges, those Buddhas likewise each raise their voices to proclaim the name of the Tathāgata Śākyamuni for their respective assemblies."
At that time, the great bodhisattvas of that buddha-field, having heard this, each addressed the Buddha, saying:
"It is rare, World-Honored One!
We now wish to go to the Sahā world to see the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, to pay him homage and make offerings, and to hear what we have not yet heard."
Then those Buddhas each addressed their respective great bodhisattvas, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!
O son of noble family!"
"You should know that this is the time; you must follow these two great youths and go together with them. Why is this?

That Buddha, the World-Honored One, is difficult to encounter and difficult to behold; it is likewise exceedingly rare to hear and receive his Dharma, or to sit together in assembly among his multitude."

At that time, Śākyamuni—the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha—arose from the Samādhi of Power-Adornment and, walking slowly and steadily like a king of geese, gazed with upright composure toward the lion throne.
Having arrived and ascended, he personally spread out his *niṣīdana* mat; having laid it down, he sat upright in the full lotus posture, while the entire assembly surrounded him on all four sides.

At that time, the youth Mañjuśrī and the youth Jñānacakra-sāgara-pratibhāna, together with an assembly of immeasurable, incalculable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of great bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, returned from the east and arrived before the World-Honored One, Śākyamuni Buddha.
Those two youths and the other bodhisattvas each bowed their heads at the soles of the Buddha’s feet in prostration; having finished their salutations, they all withdrew and sat upon lotus thrones.

At that time, the Buddha addressed the Elder Ānanda: "You should now summon the bhikṣus to assemble.
Having received the Buddha’s instruction, Ānanda immediately went from place to place and announced to the bhikṣus, saying these words:
"You all should know:
the World-Honored One, the Guide, now summons you; you should go.

When the bhikṣus heard these words, they all went together. They saw the Buddha seated upon the lion throne, his radiant countenance preeminent and his majestic virtue most supreme. Joining their palms and bowing their heads, they prostrated at the Buddha’s feet. Having completed their salutations, they circumambulated him to the right and each sat down within a lotus seat.
At that time, the entire trichiliocosm was filled everywhere with exquisite lotus flowers; these blossoms were all fully opened, each resembling a jeweled throne.
Furthermore, in this world there were celestial sandalwood trees, *mandārava* trees, and celestial incense trees, and every one of these forest trees was seven *tāla* trees in height.

The branches and leaves of those trees were entirely lotus flowers; within all the lotus flowers sat bodhisattvas in the full lotus posture, and these five hundred arhats and śrāvakas likewise sat cross-legged upon lotus thrones. Even unto the Summit of Existence (*bhavāgra*), in all the palaces, groves, and gardens of the devas and nāgas, there were lotus flowers, and they too each sat atop lotus flowers.
At that time, various kinds of celestial incense and sandalwood blended together, pervading this trichiliocosm with their pervasive fragrance.
Those who smelled it felt love and joy, becoming delighted and serene;
as the fragrant breeze touched their bodies, it was cool, refreshing, and harmonious, causing all sentient beings to rejoice.
At that time, the Tathāgata sat upon the lion throne and entered the *chāyā-pratibhāsa-samādhi*.
Through the power and conditions of this samādhi, all sentient beings within every Buddha-field in the eastern direction conceived this thought:
"The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, is now facing me alone; he has compassion for me, knows my mind, and understands my speech."
"Because he knows my mind and has compassion for me, he preaches the Dharma to me according to my own disposition, and not for anyone else.
Likewise, all sentient beings in the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, above, and below—even including the gods, nāgas, and spirits up to the summit of existence—all think thus:
"The Buddha is addressing me alone, and not anyone else."
The teaching of the Dharma and the knowledge of the minds [of others] are likewise so.

At that time, the youth Mañjuśrī rose respectfully upon a lotus flower, bared his right shoulder, and, facing the Tathāgata, prostrated with single-minded devotion. Kneeling on his right knee with palms joined, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"O Great Sage, World-Honored One!"
All the foolish beings in the world do not believe such profound and wondrous words:

that the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha has awakened to and attained the wisdom of a Tathāgata—wisdom of mastery, immeasurable wisdom, unequaled wisdom, incalculable wisdom, asaṃkhyeya wisdom, great wisdom, Buddha-wisdom, and all-encompassing wisdom (sarvākārajñatā).
The Buddha said, "So it is, so it is, Mañjuśrī!"
All worlds are inconceivable;

likewise, the awakening to bodhi by the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, as well as the wisdom of the Tathāgata up to the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā), are also in this way inconceivable.
Listen attentively, listen attentively, Mañjuśrī!

Suppose there were a person in the world who took all the land of as many trichiliocosms as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River and ground it entirely into dust. Having combined these particles into a single mass, he blew upon them with his mouth once, causing each particle to return to its original realm exactly as it was before, without any increase or decrease.
"What do you think,
Mañjuśrī? Is this credible?"
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
This matter is difficult to believe; among the sentient beings of the world, there are truly none who would have faith.”
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī: “It is so, it is so.

Just as I have now spoken, this Tathāgata-knowledge—up to and including the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā)—which is awakened by the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, is likewise difficult for all sentient beings in the world to believe.”
"Furthermore, Mañjuśrī!

Suppose there were a person in this world who, using his cupped hands, took up all the calamitous waters within as many trichiliocosm worlds as there are grains of sand in the Ganges—waters whose surging waves reach even up to the second dhyāna—and placed them all entirely within a single small lotus stalk;
yet once they were inside, that lotus root would neither swell nor break."
"What do you think,
Mañjuśrī? Is this believable?"
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
This matter is difficult to believe; among the sentient beings of the world, there are truly none who would have faith.”
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī: “It is so, it is so.

What I have now spoken of—the wisdom of a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha who has awakened to bodhi, and even up to all-knowledge—is likewise difficult for all sentient beings in the world to believe.”
"Furthermore, Mañjuśrī!

Suppose there were a person in this world who, with all the fires of the kalpas existing within as many trichiliocosm worlds as there are grains of sand in the Ganges—fires whose flames are so fierce and blazing as to reach the Brahma-heaven—were to absorb all those fires, along with their smoke and flames, entirely into his own belly;

having done so, he might then eat a single small jujube, or a single sesame seed, or a single grain of non-glutinous rice, and yet his life-span would endure for kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, his body neither burned nor dead."
"What do you think,
Mañjuśrī? Is this credible?"
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
This matter is difficult to believe; among the sentient beings of the world, there are truly none who would believe it.”
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī: “So it is, so it is.

What I have now spoken of—the wisdom of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha who has awakened to bodhi, extending even to the knowledge of all modes—is likewise difficult for all sentient beings in the world to believe.”
"Furthermore, Mañjuśrī!

Suppose there were a person in this world who, with his hands, could catch and contain within a single small mustard seed all the winds of the four cardinal directions, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir—every fierce Vairambha wind and every wind-circle within all the trichiliocosm worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges—and yet that mustard seed would neither expand, nor widen, nor contract, nor be destroyed."
"What do you think,
Mañjuśrī? Is this credible?"
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
This matter is difficult to believe; among the sentient beings of the world, there are truly none who would believe it.”
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī: “So it is, so it is.

What I have now spoken of—the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha having awakened to Bodhi, and this wisdom of the Tathāgata up to the knowledge of all modes—is likewise difficult for all sentient beings in the world to believe.”
"Furthermore, Mañjuśrī!

Suppose there were a person in this world who, with all the space within as many trichiliocosm worlds as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, desired to sit cross-legged and fill that entire space, remaining there for either one kalpa or half a kalpa."
"What do you think,
Mañjuśrī? Is this credible?"
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
This matter is difficult to believe; among the sentient beings of the world, there are truly none who would believe it.”
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī: "So it is, so it is.

What I have now spoken of—the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, having awakened to Bodhi, and this wisdom of the Tathāgata up to the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā)—is likewise difficult for all sentient beings in the world to believe."
"Furthermore, Mañjuśrī!

Suppose there were a person in this world who, with a single thought-moment, were to gather together the minds of all sentient beings within as many trichiliocosm worlds as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, and having placed these immeasurable sentient beings' minds in one place, cause them to become a single mind."
What do you think,
Mañjuśrī? Is this credible?
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
This matter is difficult to believe; among the sentient beings of the world, there are truly none who would have faith.”
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī: “So it is, so it is.

What I have now spoken of—the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha’s awakening to this Tathāgata-knowledge up to the knowledge of all modes—is likewise difficult for all sentient beings in the world to believe.”
At that time, the youth Jñānacakra-sāgara-pratibhāna, on his lotus seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha again, saying:
“World-Honored One!

Regarding the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, who has awakened to anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi: what is the meaning of the Tathāgata’s wisdom, sovereign wisdom, inconceivable wisdom, immeasurable wisdom, unequaled wisdom, incalculable wisdom, asaṃkhyeya wisdom, great wisdom, Buddha-wisdom, and all-aspect wisdom?
The Buddha addressed the youth Jñānacakra-sāgara-pratibhāna, saying:
"Good son, listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect well upon it; I shall analyze and explain it for you."
“Good son! Because all sentient beings are equal, all dharmas are also equal; this is the wisdom of the Tathāgata.
Because all dharmas are equal, all sentient beings are also equal; this is suchness that is non-different from suchness, suchness that is truly suchness. Wisdom-Wheel Youth!”
One should know that this is called the wisdom of the Tathāgata.
By reason of this wisdom, the Tathāgata truly knows the knowledge of what is possible and what is impossible, as well as the knowledge of what is possible and what is impossible.
"Furthermore, Child Jñānacakra-sāgara-pratibhāna!
Because the Tathāgata knows that all sentient beings arise through mastery, all phenomena likewise arise through mastery;
because all phenomena arise spontaneously through causes and conditions, all sentient beings likewise arise spontaneously through causes and conditions."
This is the wisdom of the Tathāgata. Why is this?
All sentient beings are not self-made, nor made by another; they are not of the past, the present, or the future; when sought, they cannot be found.
Why is this? Because there is no agent.
Since there is no agent, all sentient beings are empty in the past, empty in the present, and empty in the future as well; such is the nature of sentient beings, for they lack an agent.
All dharmas are likewise thus: there is no past, future, or present agent.
Why is this? Because an agent is entirely non-existent.
If anyone should say,
"There is an agent," you should know that this person speaks falsely and deceptively.
O Youthful Cakra!
You should know that this is called the Tathāgata’s sovereign wisdom.
By reason of this wisdom, the Tathāgata truly knows the destination of all karmic actions.
Furthermore, O Youth of Eloquence, Ocean of the Wheel of Wisdom!

Because the Tathāgata possesses the inconceivable wisdom regarding all sentient beings, and because he possesses the inconceivable wisdom regarding all phenomena just as he does regarding all sentient beings;
thus, he possesses the inconceivable knowledge of all sentient beings and the inconceivable knowledge of all phenomena.
Why is this? It is because that mental consciousness cannot be seen or known by any sentient beings.
Just like space, it is without distinction and cannot be perceived; the true essence of all sentient beings is inconceivable.
In this way, because the causal conditions for the true meaning of all sentient beings are inconceivable, all phenomena are also inconceivable;
and just as all phenomena are inconceivable, so too are all sentient beings inconceivable.
O Youth Jñānacakra!
You should know that this is called the inconceivable wisdom of the Tathāgata.
By reason of this wisdom, the Tathāgata truly knows all causes and conditions of defilement and purity, as well as their karmic fruits and retributions, in the past, the present, and the future.
"Furthermore, O Youth of Wisdom-Wheel Ocean Eloquence!
Because the Tathāgata knows that all sentient beings are immeasurable, he possesses the wisdom that all phenomena are likewise immeasurable;
because all phenomena are immeasurable, he possesses the wisdom that all sentient beings are likewise immeasurable."

Why is this? It is because the mind, intellect, and consciousness of all sentient beings are neither visible nor knowable; they are as immeasurable as space and as unfathomable as the true nature of all sentient beings.
In this way, because all sentient beings are immeasurable, all phenomena are also immeasurable;
because all phenomena are immeasurable, all sentient beings are also immeasurable.
O Youth Jñānacakra!
You should know that this is called the Tathāgata’s inconceivable wisdom.
By reason of this wisdom, the Tathāgata truly knows all sentient beings, including the differences in their faculties and their degrees of diligence.
"Furthermore, Jñānacakra-sāgara-pratibhāna-kumāra!
Because the Tathāgata knows all sentient beings to be equal, he possesses the wisdom of the equality of all phenomena;
because all phenomena are equal, he also possesses the wisdom of the equality of all sentient beings."
Why is this? If the essential nature of nirvāṇa were different from that of all sentient beings, then the analogy would be inconsistent.
One should know this:
Nirvāṇa and sentient beings are one and not two; for the essential nature of all sentient beings is no different from nirvāṇa, yet it is not that they are not different from suchness (tathatā).
Because all sentient beings are equal, all phenomena are also equal;
because all phenomena are not [inherently] equal, there is likewise no wisdom that perceives all sentient beings as [inherently] equal.
"O Youth Jñānacakra!
You should know that this is called the Tathāgata’s unequaled wisdom.
By reason of this unequaled wisdom, the Tathāgata truly knows the immeasurable realms and various realms of all sentient beings."
"Furthermore, Jñānacakra-sāgara-pratibhāna-kumāra!
Because the Tathāgata knows that all sentient beings are incalculable by way of causes and conditions, he possesses the wisdom that all phenomena are incalculable;
because all phenomena are incalculable by way of causes and conditions, he also possesses the wisdom that all sentient beings are incalculable."
Just as the essence and nature of the dharma-realm is incalculable, so too, O Youth of the Ocean-like Eloquence of the Wisdom-Wheel!
because all sentient beings are detached from their own individual natures, they are incalculable; likewise, all dharmas are also incalculable.
Furthermore, because all sentient beings are incalculable, all dharmas are incalculable, and even unto all sentient beings themselves are incalculable.
O Youth Jñānacakra!
You should know that this is called the Tathāgata’s incalculable wisdom.
By reason of this incalculable wisdom, the Tathāgata truly knows the various inclinations toward pleasure in all sentient beings.
"Furthermore, Jñānacakra-sāgara-pratibhāna-kumāra!
Because the Tathāgata knows the incalculable causes and conditions of all sentient beings, he possesses incalculable wisdom regarding all phenomena;
because he knows the incalculable causes and conditions of all phenomena, he possesses incalculable wisdom regarding all sentient beings."
Furthermore, because of the incalculable causes and conditions of all sentient beings, there is incalculable wisdom regarding all phenomena.
Child Jñānacakra,
you should know that this is called the Tathāgata’s incalculable wisdom.

Due to these causes and conditions of incalculable wisdom, the Tathāgata truly knows all meditative concentrations, liberations, samādhis, samāpattis, the cessation of afflictions, their arousal, and their abandonment.
"Furthermore, Jñānacakra-sāgara-pratibhāna-kumāra!
Because the Tathāgata knows all sentient beings to be great, he also possesses the great wisdom regarding all phenomena;
because he possesses the great wisdom regarding all phenomena, he also possesses the great wisdom regarding all sentient beings, free from all obstructions."
"Free from obstacles" is a name for all sentient beings;
furthermore, "free from obstacles" means being free from darkness.
Being free from darkness is called the radiance of the luminous essence.
That which is brilliantly illuminating has no defilement regarding any objective realm;
because it is free from defilement, it is called "free from obstruction.
The great realm of sentient beings is one and without difference; this is called the "great realm of the essential nature of sentient beings."
Because all sentient beings are the causal conditions for the Great Boundary, they are also "Great" because all phenomena are free from defilement and non-different;
and because all phenomena are great, all sentient beings are great.
It should be known that all phenomena, being free from dust and defilement, are free from darkness.
If anyone were to say,
"There is the arising of darkness in all things," such a thing is impossible.
"O Youth Jñānacakra!
This is called the Tathāgata’s Great Wisdom that is Free from Darkness.

Furthermore, by virtue of this great wisdom, the Tathāgata perceives with his divine eye the birth and death of all sentient beings—whether they are currently born among gods or humans, or will be born in the hells, as animals, or as hungry ghosts—and he truly knows how sentient beings undergo rebirth through the causal conditions of their remaining karma."
"Furthermore, Jñānacakra-sāgara-pratibhāna-kumāra!

Because the Tathāgata knows the causes and conditions of all sentient beings of the past, present, and future, he possesses the Tathāgata’s wisdom regarding all phenomena of the past, present, and future;
and because he knows the causes and conditions of all phenomena of the past, present, and future, he possesses the Tathāgata’s wisdom regarding all sentient beings of the past, present, and future."
Jñānacakra!
Just as the dharma-realm of the three periods—past, present, and future—is invisible, at that time the sentient-being realm of the three periods—past, present, and future—is also invisible;
just as the sentient-being realm of the three periods—past, present, and future—is invisible, at that time the entire dharma-realm of the three periods—past, present, and future—is also invisible.
This invisible dharma-nature, the essence of dharmas, and all Buddha-bodies as well as non-Buddha-bodies, sentient beings' bodies, and so forth, are of one kind and without difference.
O Youthful Jñānacakra!
You should know that this is called the Tathāgata’s Buddha-wisdom.
By reason of this wisdom, the Tathāgata truly knows all birth and death throughout the three periods of time.
Furthermore, O Youth of Eloquence, Ocean of the Wheel of Wisdom!
Because the Tathāgata knows all sentient beings through all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), the Tathāgata possesses all-aspect knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*) regarding all phenomena;
because the Tathāgata possesses all-knowledge regarding all phenomena, the Tathāgata possesses all-aspect knowledge regarding all sentient beings;
and because he possesses all-knowledge regarding all sentient beings, it is the wisdom of the Tathāgata.
By reason of the Tathāgata’s wisdom, the all-knowledge of all sentient beings is the Tathāgata’s wisdom.
Wisdom-Wheel Youth!
Because all sentient beings possess all-knowledge, it is the Tathāgata’s wisdom.
In this way, the wisdom of the Tathāgata is the all-knowledge of all sentient beings.

In this way, because of the causal conditions for the all-knowledge of all phenomena, and because of the causal conditions for the all-knowledge of the Tathāgata, there is even the all-knowledge of all phenomena.
Thus it is, Jñānacakra!

These Buddhas of the past, future, and present—the Tathāgata’s omniscience of the past, omniscience of the future, and omniscience of the present—are so called because this wisdom is all-encompassing. Therefore, the Tathāgata possesses the knowledge of the meaning of births in the past, the knowledge of the meaning of births in the future, and the knowledge of the meaning of births in the present.
Jñānacakra! This is called the Tathāgata’s knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā).
Because it is the causal condition for this knowledge of all modes, the Tathāgata possesses the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows (āsravakṣayajñāna), which is true knowledge.
"What is this wisdom?
The past world is empty, the future world is empty, and the present world is empty; all three times are empty.
It is without arising and without ceasing, without abiding and without change, neither identical nor different, but suchness (tathatā); this is called the Tathāgata’s wisdom."
The absence of causal conditions is called sovereign wisdom;
being free from the spheres of mind, intellect, and consciousness, it is called inconceivable wisdom;
because space is without differentiation, it is called immeasurable wisdom.
Because its causes and conditions are peerless, it is called "peerless wisdom";
because the dharma-realm is incalculable, it is called "incalculable wisdom";
because its causes and conditions are *asaṃkhyeya* upon *asaṃkhyeya*, it is called "*asaṃkhyeya* wisdom."
Because it is free from obstructive causes and conditions, it is called Great Wisdom;
because it is the cause and condition for the Buddhas of the past, future, and present, it is called Buddha-Wisdom;
and because it is the cause and condition for all existing wisdoms of the past, present, and future, it is called the Tathāgata’s Knowledge of All Modes (sarvākārajñatā).

"This omniscience, the locus of omniscience, as well as names, phrases, and syllables—all words and speech arising from the conjunction of causes and conditions—I shall now briefly explain word by word:

the supreme *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* wisdom that accords with the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha in all respects; this is called the Tathāgata’s wisdom, the sovereign wisdom, the inconceivable wisdom, the immeasurable wisdom, the unequaled wisdom, the incalculable wisdom, the *asaṃkhyeya* wisdom, the great wisdom, the Buddha-wisdom, and the wisdom of all modes (*sarvākāra-jñāna*)."
At that time, the youth Jñānacakra-sāgara-pratibhāna addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
how is it that because the power of sentient beings arises through causes and conditions, the power of the Tathāgata also arises?”
"Because the power of the Tathāgata arises, does the power of sentient beings also arise?
The Buddha said, "It is so, Cakracitra!
Because the power of the Tathāgata arises, the power of sentient beings also arises."
The power of the Tathāgata and the power of sentient beings—because these two powers are not different from one another, they are called the "one realm of suchness" (ekadhātu-tathatā).
Through the conditions of the power of sentient beings, the power of the Tathāgata arises;
through the conditions of the power of the Tathāgata, the power of sentient beings arises.
"Therefore, the Tathāgata possesses the awakening of all-knowledge.
At that time, the youth Prajñācakravaramahāsāgarapratibhāna addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"How, O Jñānacakra, is the omniscience (sarvajñajñāna) of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha produced?
The Buddha said:
"It is produced from the twelve links of dependent origination (dvādaśāṅgapratītyasamutpāda), Jñānacakra."
The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha gives birth to the knowledge of all modes.
O Jñānacakra youth!
The twelve links of dependent origination are as follows: namely, eye and form, ear and sound, nose and odor, tongue and taste, body and touch, mind and mental phenomena.

"Because of this knowledge of causes and conditions (*hetupratyaya-jñāna*), the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*) arises; it is said that because of the knowledge of causes and conditions, one fears arising from causes and conditions.
At that time, the youth Prajñācakrasāgarapratibhāna addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!..."

The immeasurable Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas—possessing the eye of all-knowledge, the form of all-knowledge, the ear of all-knowledge, the sound of all-knowledge, the nose of all-knowledge, the fragrance of all-knowledge, the tongue of all-knowledge, the taste of all-knowledge, the body of all-knowledge, the touch of all-knowledge, the mind of all-knowledge, and the phenomena of all-knowledge?
Having been asked thus, the Buddha replied to the youth Jñānacakra-sāgara-pratibhāna:

“There are immeasurable all sentient beings; the eyes of all sentient beings, the forms of all sentient beings, the ears of all sentient beings, the sounds of all sentient beings, the noses of all sentient beings, the fragrances of all sentient beings, the tongues of all sentient beings, the tastes of all sentient beings, the bodies of all sentient beings, the tangibles of all sentient beings, the minds of all sentient beings, and the phenomena of all sentient beings.”
Thus it is, O youth Jñānacakra!

The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha possesses the eye of all-knowledge, the form of all-knowledge, the ear of all-knowledge, the sound of all-knowledge, the nose of all-knowledge, the fragrance of all-knowledge, the tongue of all-knowledge, the taste of all-knowledge, the body of all-knowledge, the touch of all-knowledge, the mind of all-knowledge, and the phenomena of all-knowledge.

The immeasurable Tathāgatas possess the eye of all-knowledge, the form of all-knowledge, the ear of all-knowledge, the sound of all-knowledge, the nose of all-knowledge, the fragrance of all-knowledge, the tongue of all-knowledge, the taste of all-knowledge, the body of all-knowledge, the touch of all-knowledge, the mind of all-knowledge, and the phenomena of all-knowledge.

In this same way, all sentient beings also possess the eye of all-knowledge, the form of all-knowledge, the ear of all-knowledge, the sound of all-knowledge, the nose of all-knowledge, the fragrance of all-knowledge, the tongue of all-knowledge, the taste of all-knowledge, the body of all-knowledge, the touch of all-knowledge, the mind of all-knowledge, and the phenomena of all-knowledge.
The Buddha said to Jñānacakra, "What do you think?
Is there even a single form that is not seen by the eyes of sentient beings?"
Jñānacakra said:
“World-Honored One!
There is not a single form that is not seen by the eyes of sentient beings; it is simply that you cause all such forms to be fully beheld.”
The Buddha said,
“Jñānacakra! Is there not such form in the world that is likewise unseen by the eyes of sentient beings?”
Jñānacakra said:
"World-Honored One!
There is no such sentient being who does not see this form."
The Buddha said,
“Jñānacakra! There is no such form in the world that even the eye of omniscience does not see.”
O Youth Jñānacakra!
You should know that this skillful means is the eye of all immeasurable sentient beings; likewise, it is the eye of omniscience.
It is the form of all immeasurable sentient beings; likewise, it is the form of omniscience.
"Furthermore, Jñānacakra-sāgara-pratibhāna-kumāra!
Within this world, is there even a single sound that is not heard by the auditory consciousness of all sentient beings?"
Jñānacakra said:
“World-Honored One!
There is no such sound that is not heard by the ears of sentient beings.”
The Buddha said,
“Jñānacakra! There is no such sound in the world that even the ears of the Omniscient One do not hear.”
O Youth Jñānacakra!
You should know that this skillful means is the ear of all immeasurable sentient beings; likewise, it is the ear of omniscience.
It is the voice of all immeasurable sentient beings; likewise, it is the voice of omniscience.
"Furthermore, Jñānacakra-sāgara-pratibhāna-kumāra!
Within this world, is there even a single fragrance that is not smelled by the noses of all sentient beings?"
Jñānacakra said:
“World-Honored One!
There is no such fragrance that is not smelled by the noses of sentient beings.”
The Buddha said,
“Jñānacakra! There is no such fragrance in the world that even the nose of one possessing all-knowledge would not be perfumed by.”
O Youth Jñānacakra!
You should know that this skillful means is such that the noses of all immeasurable sentient beings are the nose of omniscience;
likewise, the fragrances of all immeasurable sentient beings are the fragrance of omniscience.
"Furthermore, Jñānacakra-sāgara-pratibhāna-kumāra!
Is there any single flavor in the world that is not tasted by the tongues of all sentient beings?"
Jñānacakra said:
“World-Honored One!
There is no such flavor that is not tasted by the tongues of sentient beings.”
The Buddha said,
“Jñānacakra! There is no such flavor in the world that even the tongue of the Omniscient One has not tasted.”
O Youth Jñānacakra!
You should know that by this skillful means, the tongues of all immeasurable sentient beings are, in this way, the tongue of omniscience;
the tastes of all immeasurable sentient beings are, in this way, the taste of omniscience.
"Furthermore, Jñānacakra-sāgara-pratibhāna-kumāra!
Within the world, is there even a single touch that is not perceived within the bodies of all sentient beings?"
Jñānacakra said:
“World-Honored One!
There is no such contact that is not perceived by the bodies of sentient beings.”
The Buddha said:
“Jñānacakra! There is no such contact in the world that even the body of the Omniscient One does not perceive.”
O Youth Jñānacakra!
You should know that through this skillful means, the bodies of all immeasurable sentient beings are thus the body of omniscience;
the touches of all immeasurable sentient beings are thus the touch of omniscience.
"Furthermore, Jñānacakra-sāgara-pratibhāna-kumāra!
Is there even a single phenomenon in the world that is not known within the minds of all sentient beings?"
Jñānacakra said:
“World-Honored One!
There is no such dharma that is not known by the minds of sentient beings.”
The Buddha said,
“Jñānacakra! There is no such phenomenon in the world that even the mind of the Omniscient One does not know.”
O Youth Jñānacakra!
You should know that by this skillful means, one knows the minds of all immeasurable sentient beings; such is the mind of omniscience.
One knows the dharmas of all immeasurable sentient beings; such is the dharma of omniscience.
In this way, the mind of all sentient beings is the mind of omniscience;
the phenomena of all sentient beings are the phenomena of omniscience.
These two kinds are not different in the slightest.
"Furthermore, Jñānacakra-sāgara-pratibhāna-kumāra!

Just as the eyes of all sentient beings and the forms of all sentient beings, up to the minds of all sentient beings and the phenomena of all sentient beings, and the eye of omniscience and the forms of omniscience, up to the mind of omniscience and the phenomena of omniscience—these two extremes are one single dharma-realm."
“Jñānacakra!

In this way, the eyes of all immeasurable sentient beings are like the eye of omniscience; even so, the mental phenomena of all immeasurable sentient beings are like the mental phenomena of omniscience.”
In this way, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha possesses the eye-knowledge and the knowledge of the afflictions of the eye,
the knowledge of the cessation of the eye and the knowledge of the cessation of the afflictions of the eye; likewise,
he possesses the form-knowledge and the knowledge of the afflictions of form, the knowledge of the cessation of form and the knowledge of the cessation of the afflictions of form.
Knowledge of the ear, knowledge of defilements regarding the ear, knowledge of the cessation of the ear, and knowledge of the cessation of defilements regarding the ear;
knowledge of sound, knowledge of defilements regarding sound, knowledge of the cessation of sound, and knowledge of the cessation of defilements regarding sound;
knowledge of the nose, knowledge of defilements regarding the nose, knowledge of the cessation of the nose, and knowledge of the cessation of defilements regarding the nose.
Knowledge of fragrance, knowledge of the afflictions of fragrance, knowledge of the cessation of fragrance, and knowledge of the cessation of the afflictions of fragrance;
knowledge of the tongue, knowledge of the afflictions of the tongue, knowledge of the cessation of the tongue, and knowledge of the cessation of the afflictions of the tongue;
knowledge of taste, knowledge of the afflictions of taste, knowledge of the cessation of taste, and knowledge of the cessation of the afflictions of taste.
Knowledge of the body, knowledge of the afflictions of the body, knowledge of the cessation of the body, and knowledge of the cessation of the afflictions of the body;
knowledge of contact, knowledge of the afflictions of contact, knowledge of the cessation of contact, and knowledge of the cessation of the afflictions of contact;
knowledge of the mind, knowledge of the afflictions of the mind, knowledge of the cessation of the mind, and knowledge of the cessation of the afflictions of the mind.

The knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), the knowledge of the afflictions of phenomena (*dharmakleśajñāna*), the knowledge of the cessation of phenomena (*dharmanirodhajñāna*), and the knowledge of the cessation of the afflictions of phenomena (*dharmakleśanirodhajñāna*) are not different from one another.
Because they are not different, the eye of all sentient beings is the eye of omniscience; likewise, the phenomena of all sentient beings are the phenomena of omniscience.
This is the single Dharma-realm.
"O Youthful Jñānacakra!
It is, for example, like a wise person in the world who knows suffering for himself, knows pleasure for himself, knows that which is neither suffering nor pleasure for himself."
Why is this? Because one experiences it oneself.
O Youthful Jñānacakra!

In this way, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha fully knows the eye-wisdom, form-wisdom, ear-wisdom, sound-wisdom, nose-wisdom, fragrance-wisdom, tongue-wisdom, taste-wisdom, body-wisdom, touch-wisdom, mind-wisdom, dharma-wisdom, affliction-wisdom, cessation-wisdom, and the wisdom regarding both afflictions and their cessation of all sentient beings.
Why is this? Because of the attainment of all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*).
"The knowledge of the twelve bases (*āyatana*) of all sentient beings is called the name of the Tathāgata; the entry of all sentient beings is the form (*rūpa*) of the Tathāgata."
"All the bodily actions of the Tathāgata follow wisdom throughout the three periods of time;
all his verbal actions and all his mental actions likewise follow wisdom throughout the three periods of time."
The Tathāgata fully knows all sensations through the manifestation of all-aspect wisdom;
the Tathāgata correctly knows all things through omniscience and correctly knows all things through all-aspect wisdom; by means of all-aspect wisdom, the Tathāgata knows conditioned formations.

The Tathāgata, having known through his omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) and knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*), perceives that therein all sentient beings possess four aggregates (*skandha*) apart from form; this is called the "name" of the Tathāgata. Furthermore, he perceives the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) of all sentient beings as the "form" of the Tathāgata.
By virtue of such name and form, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, is named the Omniscient One, the All-Seeing One, the All-Touching One, and the All-Awakened One.
The Sūtra on the Samādhi of the Array of Power, Middle Volume;
The Sūtra on the Samādhi of the Array of Power, Lower Volume.
