At that time, the Buddha addressed the youth Jñānacakra-sāgarapratibhāna, saying:
"Good son, do you see the bodies of all the Tathāgatas?
The youth Jñānacakra then replied to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!
I have seen it.
The Buddha asked Zhilun:
“You speak of a ‘seer’; what is it that is seen?
Jñānacakra replied, “World-Honored One!”
"I see all the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas.
In as many worlds as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, within those lands I also see as many Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, each preaching the Dharma within their own buddha-fields.
Thus, when the second and third Buddhas asked in this manner, the youth Jñānacakra answered in the same way.
At that time, the Buddha again asked Jñānacakra:
"Good son, do you see the palm of the Tathāgata’s right hand?"
Jñānacakra said, “I see.
The Buddha said:
“Jñānacakra! As for what you say regarding ‘the seer,’ what is it that is seen?
Jñānacakra replied:
“World-Honored One!
I see that all Buddhas, Tathāgatas, likewise speak various dharmas with the palms of their right hands upon each of those lands.”
“Jñānacakra, youth!

By such skillful means, you should know that the minds and mental factors of all sentient beings, as well as their phenomena, are the name of this Tathāgata; and the eyes, forms, ears, sounds, noses, odors, tongues, tastes, bodies, and tangibles of all sentient beings are the form of this Tathāgata.
This name of the Tathāgata and this form are called the ‘all-knowledge’ (sarvajñatā) of the Tathāgata, and are also called ‘all-seeing’ (sarvadṛk).”
At that time, the youth Jñānacakra-sāgara-pratibhāna addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
That which the Tathāgata has spoken is inconceivable—the subtle, supreme, and most inconceivable realm of the Tathāgata."
The Buddha said, "So it is, so it is, Youthful Jñānacakra!
The realm of the Tathāgata— the inconceivable, subtle, and most supreme— is truly inconceivable."
“O Youth Jñānacakra!
Seated beneath the Aśvattha tree, I contemplated anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; having awakened, I attained all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā).”
"O Youth Jñānacakra!
I have conceived this thought:
'Inconceivable, subtle, and most supreme inconceivable—this is the realm of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas.'"

"Having formed this inconceivable thought at that time, I rose from beneath the Aśvattha tree; neither too near nor too far, I stood facing that tree, contemplating it with single-minded attention, gazing steadily without blinking.
Sustained by the food of joy, free from other food and drink, I remained thus for seven days and seven nights, beholding the Aśvattha Bodhi tree."

Once I have sat thus beneath this tree, no one in all the worlds will be able to believe that the Buddha has attained the wisdom of a Tathāgata, the wisdom of mastery, the inconceivable wisdom, the immeasurable wisdom, the unequaled wisdom, the incalculable wisdom, the asaṃkhyeya wisdom, the great wisdom, the Buddha-wisdom, and the wisdom of all modes.
"Furthermore, Jñānacakra!

Opposite the Aśvattha Bodhi tree, there is a stūpa at that very spot called Animiṣanayanadarśana (The One Beheld with Unblinking Eyes). It was here that my inconceivable mind beheld the Aśvattha Bodhi tree and gave rise to unblinking eyes; for seven days, I partook of the food of joy and remained free from the thought of other food. That great caitya has been constantly venerated by devas and humans."
"O Youth Jñānacakra!
You should know that such skillful means are the inconceivable, profound realm of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas.
Furthermore, O Jñānacakra!"

You should not now harbor such thoughts, thinking that after the Tathāgata had awakened to Bodhi, he remained alone by the Āśvattha tree for seven days and nights, gazing at it with an unblinking eye, subsisting on the food of joy and abstaining from all other food.
O Youth Jñānacakra!
Be careful not to give rise to such a thought. Why is this?

All the Buddhas of the past in the ten directions—the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas—who have now entered the nirvana of tranquil extinction: those Tathāgatas likewise each sat beneath the Bodhi tree; having sat there, they all attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā), and all gave rise to this inconceivable mind, this most supreme and inconceivable mind, the profound realm of the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas.

Those Buddhas likewise each gave rise to such inconceivable thoughts: from beneath their respective bodhi trees, they rose and went elsewhere, gazing fixedly at this tree with unblinking eyes; they obtained the food of joy and were free from other food;
they remained for seven days and nights, and it was just so.
“O Youth Jñānacakra!

In future ages, all the Buddhas, Tathāgatas of the ten directions shall likewise sit beneath the Bodhi tree, attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, and realize the inconceivable All-Knowledge (sarvajñatā), even unto the supreme and inconceivable realm of the Tathāgata.”

That Buddha, the Tathāgata, likewise gave rise to an inconceivable mind directed toward the Bodhi tree; observing the tree, he remained with unblinking eyes, attained the food of joy, and was free from the perception of other foods;
he remained thus for seven days and nights, and it was exactly the same as before.
“Jñānacakra, youth!

If all the Buddhas of the ten directions currently abide in the world and even preach the Dharma, those Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, likewise sit beneath the Bodhi tree; having attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and all-knowledge (sarvajñatā), they also reflect in this way, up to the greatest inconceivable realm of the Tathāgata.”

After that Buddha, the Tathāgata, had attained the inconceivable mind, he arose from beneath the Bodhi tree and gazed at the Bodhi tree with unblinking eyes; having attained the food of joy, he was free from all other food and drink;
he remained thus for seven days and nights, and it was likewise so thereafter.
At that time, the youth Jñānacakra-sāgara-pratibhāna again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

How is it that the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas—all Buddhas—having attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and all-knowledge (sarvajñatā) beneath the Bodhi tree, form such inconceivable thoughts and likewise contemplate in this way; gazing at the Bodhi tree without blinking, obtaining the food of joy and remaining apart from other food and drink, they abide in this place for either two or seven days?”
The Buddha said to the youth Jñānacakra:
"Son of good family,
it is not the case that all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas remain before the Bodhi tree for seven days and seven nights without blinking their eyes."
O Youth Jñānacakra!

There are Buddhas, Tathāgatas, who have attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; from the time they have awakened until they enter the untainted (anāsrava) nirvāṇa, this interval is inconceivable, and the realm of mindfulness of the Buddha is inconceivable.
"O Youth Jñānacakra!
You should understand this skillful means in this way:
the Buddhas constantly keep in mind the inconceivable realm of all Buddhas, the most supreme and inconceivable realm of the Tathāgatas."
The youth Jñānacakra again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
What is the extent of the realm of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha?"
The Buddha told Jñānacakra:
"The realm of all Buddhas is based upon the realm of all sentient beings.
The youth Jñānacakra again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How great is the scope of the realm of all sentient beings?
The Buddha told Zhilun:
"In this way, all such realms of the Buddhas are called the realm of all sentient beings.
Furthermore, Jñānacakra!
You should now know:
"The realm of all Buddhas and the realm of all sentient beings—these two realms are one single Dharma-realm, without any distinction.
The youth Jñānacakra again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"What is meant by 'Buddha,' and what is this 'Dharma'?
The Buddha told Jñānacakra:
“You should now know this:
all sentient beings are called the Buddha-dharma.
Wisdom Wheel asked again:
“What are sentient beings?
How is one called a Buddha?
The Buddha told Jñānacakra:
“Regarding the realm of sentient beings, you should know that this meaning is the domain of the Buddha.
The Buddha said to Jñānacakra, “I shall now question you; answer as you see fit.”
"What is meant by 'mind'?
For what causes and conditions does the Tathāgata attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?
The youth Jñānacakra replied:
“World-Honored One!
Because of the very nature of the self-substance of all sentient beings, you are a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.
At that time, the World-Honored One again questioned the youth Jñānacakra, saying:
“Jñānacakra! What do you think?
Do you know what the wisdom of the Tathāgata is like?”
The youth Jñānacakra immediately replied to the Buddha, saying:
“Because he knows the spheres of all sentient beings, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha is fully endowed with wisdom.”
The Buddha told Jñānacakra:
"You should know this:

by such skillful means, the realm of immeasurable Buddhas and Tathāgatas is of one kind with the realm of all sentient beings; if there is the realm of all sentient beings, that is itself the realm of the Buddha."
"In this way, the realm of all Tathāgatas and the realm of all sentient beings are a single realm; they are non-dual and without distinction.
At that time, the youth Prajñācakra-sāgara-pratibhāna addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
"As I understand the meaning and intent of what the Buddha has taught, I know that the Buddhas are not different from sentient beings, and all sentient beings are likewise the Tathāgata.
At that time, the Buddha confirmed the words of the youth Jñānacakra, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!"
"O Youth Jñānacakra!
You now well understand the meaning of the Tathāgata’s words.

Furthermore, you have in the past planted the roots of all virtues under immeasurable Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; you have heard the subtle and wondrous Dharma-gates spoken by those Buddhas, and have long cultivated the Prajñāpāramitā day and night. Throughout your successive births, you have constantly attained the analytical eloquence of meaning, the analytical eloquence of phenomena, the analytical eloquence of language, and the analytical eloquence of ready speech, remaining unimpeded in answering the questions of all sentient beings."
At that time, the youth Jñānacakra-sāgara-pratibhāna again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

How is it that the Tathāgatas and the Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are able to perform such deeds, attaining the wisdom of the Tathāgata, sovereign wisdom, inconceivable wisdom, immeasurable wisdom, unequaled wisdom, incalculable wisdom, asaṃkhyeya wisdom, great wisdom, Buddha-wisdom, and all-aspect wisdom (sarvākārajñatā), thereby reaching full understanding, realization, and awareness?”
When he had asked this, the Buddha immediately replied: “Cintāmaṇicakra,
I practice within the Prajñāpāramitā with an undistracted mind.”
O Youth Jñānacakra!

Because they practice the *prajñāpāramitā* with an undistracted mind, Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are able to attain and thus awaken to such as the Tathāgata-knowledge, sovereign knowledge, inconceivable knowledge, immeasurable knowledge, unequaled knowledge, incalculable knowledge, *asaṃkhyeya* knowledge, Buddha-knowledge, great knowledge, and the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).
The youth Jñānacakra again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

How do the Tathāgatas and the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice within the *prajñāpāramitā*? Having practiced, how is it that they neither abandon conceptualization nor practice within non-conceptualization, nor do they realize through conceptualization?”
The Buddha told Jñānacakra:

"In this regard, when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom, they practice within the eye and within forms; within the ear and within sounds; within the nose and within odors; within the tongue and within tastes; within the body and within tangibles; and within the mind and within phenomena."
The youth Jñānacakra said:

“In what way do they proceed within the eye and within forms; within the ear and within sounds; within the nose and within odors; within the tongue and within tastes; within the body and within tangibles; and within the mind and within phenomena?”
The Buddha said, “Jñānacakra!
When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva acts within the sphere of the eye and forms, one should know that this eye constitutes an obstruction for forms.”
"The ear is obstructed by sound; the nose is obstructed by fragrance; the tongue is obstructed by flavor; the body is obstructed by touch; and the mind is obstructed by mental phenomena.
Jñānacakra asked, "In what way is the eye obstructed by forms, and so on, up to how is the mind obstructed by mental phenomena?"
The Buddha said: "Jñānacakra!
Because the eye conditions visible forms, the mind gives rise to joy, or gives rise to suffering and affliction, or gives rise to equanimity."
Because the mind grasps and clings, greed, hatred, and delusion arise; through the convergence of causes and conditions, one creates various karmas of body, speech, and mind.
Having created these karmas, one takes birth within the six realms of existence—hell, hungry ghosts, animals, asuras, devas, and humans—as one's place of reliance.
Within that state, the eye and forms arise as karmic retribution; because one experiences this retribution, the ignorant person’s suffering and affliction increase and expand in future lives.
Thus, the cycle of past and future continues without ceasing, and because of these fruits, all sufferings remain unextinguished.
Why is this? Within the cycle of saṃsāra, one does not see the path leading out of it.
Ordinary beings, deluded and inverted, do not know that sound has the ear as its condition, nor do they know that mental phenomena have the mind as their condition, as explained in detail above.
"A person of wisdom should contemplate with a sincere and attentive mind:
'As for this eye, who is it that possesses this eye? What is this eye? "
He sought the meaning of "eye" and the meaning of "non-eye";

likewise, he sought the meaning of "form" and the meaning of "non-form," and so on, up to the meanings of "ear, sound, nose, fragrance, tongue, taste, body, touch, mind, and phenomena," as well as their non-meanings; yet in all these searches, he saw nothing at all.

Having reflected thus with discernment, the wise person does not perceive the meaning of the eye, nor do they perceive the meaning of what is not the eye; they do not perceive any meaning of the eye or what is not the eye. This extends even to the meaning of form (*rūpa*), which they do not perceive, nor the meaning of what is not form, nor any meaning of form or what is not form.

Likewise, regarding the ear and sound, the nose and odor, the tongue and taste, the body and tangibles, and the mind and mental objects (*dharma*): they do not perceive the meaning of these phenomena (*dharma*), nor do they perceive the meaning of what is not phenomena, nor do they perceive the meaning of both phenomena and non-phenomena.

"At that time, the practitioner does not see the eye; having already departed from the meaning of the eye, they likewise do not see 'this is the eye' or 'this is not the eye. They do not see form, nor do they see the departure from form, nor do they see 'this is form' or 'this is not form.

In this way, the ear is not the ear, and the ear is not non-ear; sound is not sound, and sound is not non-sound; the nose is not the nose, and the nose is not non-nose; fragrance is not fragrance, and fragrance is not non-fragrance; the tongue is not the tongue, and the tongue is not non-tongue; taste is not taste, and taste is not non-taste; the body is not the body, and the body is not non-body; touch is not touch, and touch is not non-touch; the mind is not the mind, and the mind is not non-mind; phenomena are not phenomena, and phenomena are not non-phenomena."
"Furthermore, the eye does not perceive, that which is not the eye does not perceive, and both the eye and what is not the eye do not perceive;
likewise, form does not perceive, that which is not form does not perceive, and both form and what is not form do not perceive;
the ear does not perceive, that which is not the ear does not perceive, and both the ear and what is not the ear do not perceive; sound does not perceive..."
...one does not perceive sound, nor does one perceive non-sound, nor does one perceive that which is neither sound nor non-sound;

the nose does not perceive, nor does it perceive non-nose, nor does it perceive that which is neither nose nor non-nose; fragrance does not perceive, nor does it perceive non-fragrance, nor does it perceive that which is neither fragrance nor non-fragrance;
the tongue does not perceive, nor does it perceive non-tongue, nor does it perceive that which is neither tongue...
The tongue does not perceive; it does not perceive flavor, nor does it perceive non-flavor, nor does it perceive both flavor and non-flavor.
The body does not perceive; it does not perceive non-body, nor does it perceive both body and non-body. Touch does not perceive;
it does not perceive non-touch, nor does it perceive both touch and non-touch. The mind does not perceive.
One does not perceive the mind, nor does one perceive what is not the mind; one does not perceive the mind as being the mind, nor does one perceive it as not being the mind.
One does not perceive dharmas, nor does one perceive non-dharmas, nor does one perceive both dharmas and non-dharmas.

"In this way, because one abandons the causal conditions of the eye, forms do not arise; because forms do not arise, one is detached from both the eye and forms. Once one is detached from the eye and forms, there is neither the pleasant nor the unpleasant."
Thus, because one is free from the pleasant and the unpleasant, where else could the pleasant and the unpleasant arise?
Because one is free from the pleasant and the unpleasant, there is no conjunction;
because there is no conjunction, it is called non-attachment and also called non-obstruction; you should know that this is precisely the wisdom of non-obstruction.
What is called unobstructed wisdom?
Unobstructed wisdom means that the eyes of all immeasurable sentient beings are the eye of omniscience; the forms of all immeasurable sentient beings are the form of omniscience.
In this way, the eye of all sentient beings is the eye of omniscience;
the form of all sentient beings is the form of omniscience.
These two kinds of phenomena are one and not different.
Because this is not awakening, in this way, the ear and sounds, up to the nose and odors, the tongue and tastes, the body and tangibles, and the mind and mental phenomena—all are non-arising.
Because causes and conditions are detached, there is no craving;
because there is no craving, one does not act within phenomena;
because one does not act within phenomena, there is no obstruction.
Because one is free from obstacles, there is no defiled attachment;
because there is no defiled attachment, one is thus free from obstacles;
and because one is free from obstacles, unimpeded wisdom arises.

By reason of wisdom, the immeasurable minds of all sentient beings are identical to the mind of omniscience; the immeasurable phenomena of all sentient beings are identical to the phenomena of omniscience.

Thus, the minds of all sentient beings and the mind of omniscience, as well as the phenomena of all sentient beings and the phenomena of omniscience—these two kinds of phenomena are one and no different.
“Jñānacakra, youth!

One practices the Prajñāpāramitā in this way: one does not practice within conceptualization, nor does one practice apart from conceptualization; one realizes it neither within conceptualization, nor does one realize it apart from conceptualization.”
O Youth Jñānacakra!
This is called the mark of the wisdom of equality regarding the minds of all sentient beings, the dharmas of all sentient beings, the mind of omniscience, and the dharmas of omniscience.
At that time, the youth Jñānacakra-sāgara-pratibhāna addressed the Buddha,
saying: “World-Honored One, regarding the dharma of non-arising, what is the meaning of the Tathāgata’s eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind— these six types of consciousness?”
The Buddha told Zhilun:
"That which is unarisen refers to the emptiness of eye-consciousness and the other [senses]; fundamentally, no entity exists therein.
When one searches within them for even a single thing, none is found; therefore, they do not arise."
Because it is unarisen, it is empty and devoid of substance.
"O Youthful Maṇicakra!
Just as space is originally unarisen, and because it is unarisen, it is without cessation;
Because it is extinguished and non-existent, there is no entity;
because it can be transcended, it is called space.
In this way, all sentient beings and all phenomena of sentient beings likewise do not arise.
Because there is no arising, there is no cessation;
furthermore, because there is no separation from phenomena, all sentient beings and all phenomena pertaining to sentient beings are like space—of one kind and without distinction.
“O Youth Jñānacakra!

All sentient beings and all phenomena of sentient beings are like space: neither arising nor ceasing, neither moving nor disturbed, neither that nor this, unstained by afflictions, and not something apart from cessation.”

Thus, it is neither arising nor ceasing, neither moving nor disordered; it is neither that nor this, neither defiled by afflictions nor detached through cessation; it is neither one nor different—emptiness is thus.
“O Youth Jñānacakra!

All sentient beings and all phenomena of sentient beings are neither born nor extinguished; they are neither moving nor chaotic; they are neither that nor this; they are not defiled by afflictions, yet they are not characterized by the departure from them through cessation.”

In this way, all Buddhas, Tathāgatas of the past, future, and present, are neither born nor extinguished; they are unmoving and undisturbed; they are neither that nor this; they are not defiled by afflictions, yet they are not a state of quiescent detachment.

This is called the abiding of the Dharma and also called the practice of the Dharma; it is suchness, neither different nor not different from suchness. Suchness is serene and eternally abiding, without transition or movement, being one with the single Dharma-realm.
At that time, the youth Jñānacakravaramahāsāgarapratibhāna again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How many Tathāgatas have already passed away in the world?”
The Buddha told the youth Jñānacakra:
"It is as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Jñānacakra asked again:
“How many Tathāgatas will appear in the future?
The Buddha said, “Jñānacakra!
“As numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Wisdom-Wheel asked again:
“How many Tathāgatas are currently preaching the Dharma?”
The Buddha said:
"O Youth Jñānacakra!
They are also as numerous as the sands of the Ganges."
The youth Jñānacakra addressed the Buddha again, saying:
“World-Honored One!
The Tathāgatas of the past have already entered parinirvāṇa; it is truly difficult to behold them again.”
The Buddhas of the future have not yet appeared in the world and thus cannot be seen in advance;
the World-Honored One of the present dwells in active teaching and has not yet entered parinirvāṇa.
That Buddha’s suchness is neither different from suchness nor not different from suchness; it is eternal, constant, and abides in the non-differentiated dharma. What is the meaning of this?
Having asked this question, the Buddha replied:
"Jñānacakra! This is the wisdom of the Buddha."
Jñānacakra! You should know that such discourse belongs to the worldly dharma and is not the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
Although such discourse exists within the dharma of *tathatā*, it cannot be realized through speech; it is that which is known and realized by the power of a Buddha’s wisdom.
"O Youth Jñānacakra!
This is called Buddha-wisdom.
What is power-wisdom?"
Because all sentient beings are equal, all phenomena are equal;
because all phenomena are equal, all sentient beings are equal in suchness (*tathatā*).
Neither different from suchness nor not different from suchness—this is called the first power of a bodhisattva mahāsattva;
by reason of this power, he knows what is possible and what is impossible as it truly is.
What are called "possible" (*sthāna*) and "impossible" (*asthāna*)?
Where there are causes and conditions, this is called "possible"; that which is devoid of causes and conditions is called "impossible.
Furthermore, O Youthful Jñānacakra!
What do you think?
Just as that which has passed away in the past is already entirely extinguished, such that it cannot be seen and cannot be known;
so too, the three types of karmic actions performed by sentient beings in the past have also passed away—do they exist or do they not exist?
The youth Jñānacakra replied to the Buddha,
“There is. The Buddha said to Jñānacakra:
"What do you think?
In a future age, when all phenomena have not yet arisen, they cannot be seen, they cannot be known, and there is not a single thing that exists."
“Will there be sentient beings with these three kinds of karmic actions in the future?
The youth Jñānacakra replied to the Buddha, “There will be.”
The Buddha said to Jñānacakra:
"What do you think?
Among the sentient beings currently existing and visible in the present world, are there any such beings who possess the three types of karmic actions?"
The youth Jñānacakra replied to the Buddha, “There is.
The Buddha said:
“Jñānacakra! What is meant by ‘existence’?
The youth Jñānacakra replied:
“World-Honored One!
Although the past ages have already passed away and ceased, the three types of karmic actions performed by sentient beings do not perish.

Furthermore, although the future has not yet come, has not yet arisen, and is not yet seen—being neither perceived nor known—nevertheless, due to causes and conditions, there are the three types of karmic actions within the future world.”

"Because of the arising of causes and conditions in the present world, because sentient beings are born, and because the three types of karma are performed, there are thus various kinds of karmic actions.
The Buddha said, "It is so."
O Youth Jñānacakra!
Because of the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā) in past ages, there were Buddhas of the past;
because of the knowledge of all modes in future ages, there will be Buddhas of the future.
Because of all the causes and conditions for the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*) within the present world, there are Buddhas in the present.
Furthermore, how is it that, because of being free from reliance on what is possible (*sthāna*) and what is impossible (*asthāna*), there is neither possibility nor impossibility?
The Buddha said:
"Jñānacakra, young man!
What do you think?"
"Just as the past void has entirely ceased and perished, is there no going,
nor any different going? The youth Jñānacakra replied, "No."
World-Honored One! Why is this?

Because it is free from dependence; because past space is the exhaustion of what is possible and what is impossible; because it is impure; because it is non-different; and because it is immovable and of an immovable nature.
The Buddha said:
"Jñānacakra, young man!
What do you think?"
"Is it as if the future were empty, unarisen, unseen, unobserved,
and unrecorded? The youth Jñānacakra replied, "No."
World-Honored One!
Why is this? Because such [realization] is free from dependence, what is possible and what is impossible will not differ in the future; it is because it is immovable and of an immovable nature.
“In this way, the present space is inexhaustible, non-different, unceasing, and immovable—an immovable dharma.
O Youthful Jñānacakra!
In this way, because the past Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, do not rely [upon anything], they are inexhaustible, non-departing, non-different, unceasing, and immovable—an immovable dharma.”

In this way, because the Buddhas and Tathāgatas of the future do not rely [on anything], they are unborn, unbecome, and do not exist through the conjunction of signs; they do not exist in another place, nor are they moving or subject to the nature of motion.

Likewise, the Buddhas and Tathāgatas of the present abide in true practice, fully comprehend and perceive the eternal, and dwell permanently in immovability; they know, as it truly is, what is possible and what is impossible.
“Jñānacakra, youth!
A bodhisattva mahāsattva should know this:
it is called the foremost power of place of all Buddhas; by reason of this power, it is that which is awakened to by the Buddha’s wisdom.”
The youth Jñānacakra again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
There is no one in all the worlds who can believe this matter of the Tathāgata.”

Furthermore, the Buddha’s knowledge of all modes is like space: it is of a single nature without distinction; it is neither born nor aged, neither dies nor is disordered; it is not subject to future birth, nor is it affliction, nor is it cessation.
Abiding in the true nature of the dharma-realm, which is suchness and equality—this is the nature of phenomena.

When the Buddha turns the wheel of Dharma, he perceives that all sentient beings undergo birth, old age, sickness, and death; thus, therein arise the causes of karma and the fruits of karma that bring about the arising and cessation of afflictions.
Having asked this question, the Buddha replied to the youth Jñānacakra:
"So it is, so it is, Jñānacakra! Youth!"

In all the worlds, there is none who can believe this; it is truly difficult to believe. Herein, only the Tathāgata has realized and known it, as well as the non-retrogressive great Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas who have planted the roots of various virtues under immeasurable Buddhas in the past—only they are able to believe this.
O Jñānacakra Kumāra!
This matter is thus, being most difficult to believe.

If there were a Tathāgata who, having awakened to *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, possesses the wisdom of a Tathāgata, sovereign wisdom, inconceivable wisdom, immeasurable wisdom, unequaled wisdom, incalculable wisdom, *asaṃkhyeya* wisdom, great wisdom, Buddha-wisdom, and all-aspect wisdom—O Jñānacakra Kumāra!
This name "Tathāgata" cannot be grasped by any in the world.
It is no different from space; so it is with all sentient beings and all phenomena.
When the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma and turns the wheel of Dharma, he speaks of the arising of existence, yet within that, there is no arising to be spoken of.

To speak of the phenomenon of aging, there is no aging; to speak of the phenomenon of affliction, there is no affliction; to speak of the phenomenon of death, there is no death; to speak of the phenomenon of outflows, there are no outflows.
To speak of non-birth, there is likewise no phenomenon of birth;
to speak of defiled afflictions, there is likewise no phenomenon of defilement.
I speak of quiescence, yet even quiescence does not exist;
I speak of nirvana, yet there is no sentient being who enters nirvana.
O Youthful Cakracara!
This is that which the Tathāgata has taught, which is difficult for all the world to believe and hard to trust.
All sentient beings are fundamentally without name; they are spoken of by means of provisional names.
They are fundamentally without speech; words are established through provisional discourse.
Fundamentally there are no words; words are established as a mere convention. Why is this?
Because through the utterance of words and phrases, one is able to know the various distinctions of all the worlds, O Child Jñānacakra!
These names, phrases, and meanings of all dharmas were previously non-existent and now exist only as provisional designations.
Child Jñānacakra!
The Dharma-wheel of the Tathāgata is likewise: it was previously non-existent and now exists.
“Jñānacakra, the Bodhisattva Youth!
The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, turn the wheel of Dharma for the sake of two great matters and conditions.
What are these two great matters and conditions?
When the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, turns the wheel of Dharma, there are two empowerments: first, the empowerment of sentient beings;
second, the empowerment of the Dharma.
"O Youthful Jñānacakra, what do you think?"
“Can it be said that sentient beings have birth?
The youth Jñānacakra replied, “No.”
“World-Honored One!
At that time, the Buddha again addressed the youth Jñānacakra:
“What do you think?”
"If all sentient beings are unarisen, could it be said that dharmas are arisen?
The youth Jñānacakra replied, "No."
"World-Honored One!
The Buddha told the youth Jñānacakra:
"Sentient beings are called 'separated from causes and conditions,' and the characteristic of sentient beings is likewise not born."
Because the mark of sentient beings is not born, all phenomena and the marks of all phenomena are likewise unborn; this unborn dharma is called "all-knowledge.
By the power of this all-encompassing wisdom, once the name of the Tathāgata Śākyamuni is heard, this trichiliocosm shakes in six ways;
at that very moment, all Buddha-fields in the ten directions shake as well, and from within the assemblies of Buddhas in such worlds, great lotus flowers emerge, each covering everything.
“O Youth Jñānacakra!
The eyes of all immeasurable sentient beings are the eye of omniscience; the forms of all immeasurable sentient beings are the form of omniscience.”
In this way, the eyes of all sentient beings are the eye of omniscience;
in this way, the forms of all sentient beings are the form of omniscience.
One should know that these two kinds are one and not two.

“The Dharma-realm is thus: the sensation of all sentient beings, the perception of all sentient beings, the formations of all sentient beings, the consciousness of all sentient beings, and the names of all sentient beings—these names are the name of the Tathāgata.”

The infinite forms of all sentient beings enter into the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), which is called the form of the Tathāgata; this form is named "all-knowledge" (*sarvajñā*), and it is also named "all-seeing," "all-consciousness," and "omniscience."

Therefore, the knowledge of all modes does not grasp at the characteristics of knowledge, nor does it cling to knowledge; this is called "all-knowledge," it is also called "all-consciousness," and it is also called "the Buddha-eye of all-seeing."
"In this way, when seeing any form, one does not grasp at its characteristics, thinking:
'My eye is able to see that.
Likewise, it is the same for forms up to mental phenomena and consciousness; the Tathāgata does not form such a thought."
"This is not consciousness.
One does not think in this way:
"This is my consciousness."
Why is this? Because the eye is not awakening, and form is not awakening; nor is it an object of awakening, up to and including the mind being not awakening, and phenomena being not awakening.
All things seen by the eyes, the Tathāgata sees and knows them all;
all echoes within the ears, he hears as all sounds;
all fragrances wafting through the nose, he smells as all scents.
Whatever is tasted within the tongue, all flavors are known;
whatever is touched within the body, all sensations are perceived;
whatever is cognized by the mind as its objects, all phenomena are attained.
Furthermore, the Tathāgata’s mindfulness is such that:

"Within the eye, all forms are seen; within the eye, all sounds are heard; within the eye, all odors are smelled; within the eye, all tastes are tasted; within the eye, all tangibles are felt; and within the eye, all phenomena are cognized."
"Thus it is, Jñānacakra!

Within the mind of the Tathāgata, all sights of form, all sounds heard, all odors smelled, all flavors tasted, all tangibles felt, and all dharmas perceived as objects exist because they accord with all sentient beings; and because the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā) can thus act as the causal condition for such wisdom."
"Jñānacakra, young man!
By such skillful means, you should know that the Tathāgata is all-knowing, all-seeing, and all-cognizing.
At that time, the youth Jñānacakra-sāgarapratibhāna addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
As I understand the meaning and intent of what the Buddha has taught, the eye is also the Tathāgata’s knowledge of all modes, and form is also the Tathāgata’s knowledge of all modes;
likewise, the ear, sound, nose, fragrance, tongue, taste, body, touch, mind, and mental phenomena are all entirely the Tathāgata’s knowledge of all modes.”
"Therefore, the Tathāgata possesses all consciousness, all vision, and all wisdom.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the youth Jñānacakra-sāgara-pratibhāna, saying: "Good son!
You have seen the Tathāgata’s universal body, universal wisdom, and the wisdom of the equality of all phenomena; what are their causes and conditions?

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva possesses the wisdom of the eyes of all sentient beings, the wisdom of the afflictions of the eyes, the wisdom of the cessation of the eyes, and the wisdom of the cessation of the afflictions of the eyes; the wisdom of the ears, the wisdom of the afflictions of the ears, the wisdom of the cessation of the ears, and the wisdom of the cessation of the afflictions of the ears; the wisdom of the nose, the wisdom of the afflictions of the nose, the wisdom of the cessation of the nose, and the wisdom of the cessation of the afflictions of the nose; the wisdom of the tongue, the wisdom of the afflictions of the tongue, the wisdom of the cessation of the tongue, and the wisdom of the cessation of the afflictions of the tongue; the wisdom of the body, the wisdom of the afflictions of the body, the wisdom of the cessation of the body, and the wisdom of the cessation of the afflictions of the body; and the wisdom of the mind, the wisdom of the afflictions of the mind, the wisdom of the cessation of the mind, and the wisdom of the cessation of the afflictions of the mind.

When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra, all the bhikṣus, all the bodhisattvas, and the entire great assembly—including devas, humans, asuras, and gandharvas—having heard the Buddha’s teaching of the Dharma, rejoiced and practiced it accordingly.
The Sūtra on the Samādhi Adorned with Powers, Scroll II.
